question: Explain the term "the preliminaries" and describe the four items of which they consist in the liturgy of the word.
idealAnswer: The sentences are scriptural passages selected to be read to the congregation at worship services. Apart from preparing the congregation for a take off in the service, they remind the worshipper of the sins which need to be confessed and of God's readiness to forgive them, and so they are not to be read for the sake of it but in a manner that appeals to the heart of the listener. Dating from the late seventh century, the readings were preceded by four distinct items, and it is these four which are known as the preliminaries: the Introit, the Kyries, the Gloria and the Collect. The Introit takes its name from the Latin introitus, meaning entry or entrance. It is a hymn or psalm sung when the ministers enter at the opening of a service, a chant which accompanied the advance of the priest to the altar. It was originally a psalm sung alternately with its antiphon, and it dates, according to older liturgists, from the fifth century and Pope Celestine 1. Sung by the choir, it announces the mystery and feast solemnized, and it also covered the entrance of the ministers, which at a solemn papal mass in a large basilica would take some time. The Kyries stand for Invocation in Greek and mean 'Lord have mercy'. Found in the Old Testament and the Gospels, they entered the liturgy late, first in the East, then in Rome in the fifth century and in Gaul in the sixth. They were the reply of the people to the litany of the deacon; Christe, eleison was later added, and in the ninth century a third series addressed to the Holy Spirit, so that the invocations became fixed at three of the Divine Person. The Gloria is an ancient hymn of praise to the Trinity, in use since the second century, whose opening line comes from Luke 2:14; it was introduced to the West by St. Hilary of Poitiers. Methodists sing it in its short form as a conclusion to canticles and psalms, in recognition of the tradition to which we belong and of the doctrine of the Trinity. The Collect, believed to have been introduced by Leo 1 or his immediate predecessor, is the prayer which gathers together the aspirations of the assembly and which the people make their own by the final Amen. Its form is an address to God, a clause referring to some attribute or saving act of God, the petition, the purpose for which we ask, and the conclusion.

topic: Outline Of The New Order For Sunday Morning Worship
question: Outline, in their proper sequence, the items of the New Order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana.
idealAnswer: The New Order for Sunday Morning Worship begins with the Call to Worship, which calls the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, and after which the choir, singing band and clergy process. This is followed by the Introit, then a Hymn, then Prayer, then a Hymn or Lyric. There follows the Ministry of the Word, which consists of the Old Testament reading, the Epistle, the Te Deum and the Gospel Reading. After the Gospel Reading comes the Affirmation of Faith, in which the Apostles' Creed is generally said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days. A Hymn follows, and then the Sermon. After the Sermon comes the Invitation to Christian Discipleship, then the Announcements, then the Tithes and Offertory, then a Hymn, and finally the Benediction and Dismissal. It should be noted that the order of service is mainly a guideline; it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, and there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility. The Te Deum, for instance, can be varied with other canticles, and where time must be saved a shorter canticle such as Canticle 6 may be sung; some canticles are occasion specific, and it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas. Choruses and canticles play the same role of singing God's praise, and one may be used in place of the other for the sake of time. The Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, so that whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction.

question: Discuss the place of the Affirmation of Faith in Methodist worship, distinguishing between the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed.
idealAnswer: The purpose of a creed is to act as a yardstick of correct belief. The creeds of Christianity have been drawn up at times of conflict about doctrine, and the acceptance or rejection of a creed serves to distinguish believers and deniers of a particular doctrine or set of doctrines. For that reason a creed was called in Greek a sumbolon, meaning half of a broken object which, when placed together with the other half, verified the bearer's identity; the Greek word passed through the Latin symbolum into the English symbol, which later took on the meaning of an outward sign of something. In the Methodist Church Ghana the Apostles' Creed is generally said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days, and preachers and liturgists should also know the other new creeds that have been added and when they are appropriate. The Apostles' Creed is the basic creed of Reformed churches and a statement of Christian belief, widely used for both liturgical and catechetical purposes. It appears to have been originally formulated as a refutation of Gnosticism, an early heresy, as can be seen in almost every phrase: it states that Christ Jesus was born, suffered and died on the cross, against the heretical teaching that Christ only appeared to become man and did not truly suffer and die. It is esteemed as an example of the apostles' teachings and a defence of the Gospel of Christ, but it does not address some Christological issues defined in the Nicene and other creeds, and says nothing explicitly about the divinity of either Jesus or the Holy Spirit. The Nicene Creed is the profession of faith most widely used in Christian liturgy. It is called Nicene because in its original form it was adopted in the city of Nicaea in 325, in the face of the Arian controversy. Arius, a Libyan preacher, had declared that although Jesus Christ was divine, God had actually created him and there was a time when he was not, which made Jesus less than the Father and contradicted the doctrine of the Trinity. The Nicene Creed therefore explicitly affirms the divinity of Jesus, applying to him the term God, and speaks of the Holy Spirit as worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son. As Methodists we recite the Nicene Creed to affirm that the doctrine of the Trinity, which makes the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit equally divine, is true. Creeds, as statements of faith, confirm the faithful in their faith and thus strengthen their corporate unity.

question: Outline the steps a Methodist preacher should follow in linking the three lessons to the theme in sermon preparation.
idealAnswer: The Methodist preacher normally has to deal with three lessons and a theme as given in the Almanac, and it is the task of the preacher to link these passages to the theme. Sermon preparation has different styles that call for different steps and procedures, and the steps recommended are not exhaustive but are deemed helpful. Step 1 is to read the passages over and over again, in different versions of the Bible including the local language, noting any translational differences that may enhance explanation and interpretation, and to meditate on the passages and the theme for some time. Step 2 is to write down your understanding of the three passages and the lessons in them, narrowing down to those lessons related to the theme. Step 3 is to select your text based on your understanding of the theme, delimiting the aspect of the theme you intend treating if the theme is broad; the text can be chosen from any of the three lessons. Step 4 is to read other parallels of your text in other books of the Bible, since the Gospels, especially the Synoptics, report almost all the events in Jesus' life but with differences which enhance interpretation, inference and implications, and the Old Testament and the Epistles also have parallels. Step 5 is to consult other materials such as Bible dictionaries, commentaries, concordances and other writings, not in order to copy other people's opinions but to help shape your own and to be relevant. Step 6 is to look critically at the background of the text and its implications for the theme and its treatment, remembering that the background of the other passages can also enhance the linkage. Step 7 is to look at the text in line with the theme and the other lessons, asking how the text treats the theme and what part of the theme the text treats. Step 8 is to consider the hows, the whys, the becauses, the therefores, the notwithstandings and the in additions. In some cases only one of the three lessons may be needed to treat the theme properly, and where the situation calls for that the preacher should not hesitate; but this is not an opportunity for lazy work. There is always a link among the three lessons in treating the theme: some links are obvious and others obscure, and the preacher must strive to unearth the link.

question: Explain the terms "exegesis" and "hermeneutics" and outline the steps which help the preacher to undertake a proper exegesis.
idealAnswer: In The Foundations of Preaching, Rev. Prof. Emmanuel Asante states that the task of the preacher is to expose the world of the Bible to his or her audience, and that this task involves the interpretation of the text, which must be considered as a process involving two approaches, namely exegesis and hermeneutics. Quoting Daniel Parte in What is Structural Exegesis, Asante defines the two terms thus: exegesis aims at understanding the text in itself, while hermeneutics attempts to elucidate what the text means for the modern interpreter and the people of his culture. Exegesis is therefore the art of critically analysing or interpreting the passage, which must be done honestly, and it must not be allowed to give way to eisegesis, the art of reading preconceived opinions into the text. The syllabus sets out points which help the preacher in sermon preparation to undertake a proper exegesis. The first is the text: the passage from which the text is chosen, and the full passage must be read. The second is the context: an overview of how the text was used in the Bible. The third is the historical setting: the historical background surrounding the text. The fourth is the geography of the land of the Bible, which may be very helpful for sermons on the baptism, transfiguration, temptation and death of Christ, since these events involve certain landmarks which, when understood, can aid in the interpretation of the events. The fifth is culture: the preacher should explain the customs and practices of the people to whom the word was originally spoken, which will help in applying the text to our modern culture. The sixth is the circumstances peculiar to the writer, that is the occasion and the target audience. Attention to these points ensures that the preacher first understands the text in itself before attempting to say what it means for the hearers of today.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the topical sermon.
idealAnswer: A topical sermon is preaching on a subject: one chooses the subject, then finds all the Scripture that relates to that subject and forms that material into a sermon. It is the most oratorical type of sermon, taking only its subject from the text, and its organization is based on the subject rather than on the distinctions of the text. It requires the preacher to have an overall knowledge of the Bible and the ability to pull together related passages from different parts of the Bible, and in preparing one the preacher must make effective use of a concordance, a dictionary or a topical Bible. Its advantages are several. First, topical sermons allow the preacher to get a grasp of a Bible subject completely, since everything about a particular subject is not found in one place in the Bible, so that the material must be collected together on purpose, analysed and preached, and in such a task the knowledge of the preacher about the whole Bible is broadened. Secondly, if there is too much Scripture to cover in one sermon, a series of sermons can be developed to cover all the passages that relate to that topic, the preacher dividing the topic into sub-topics and dealing with them in a series to ensure full coverage. Thirdly, topical sermons acknowledge and preserve the unity of the Bible, impressing on preacher and hearer alike that even though the Bible is made up of sixty-six books written by many human authors of varied backgrounds, it is one volume in unity, because the ultimate author is God Himself. Fourthly, and because of these benefits, many writers believe that topical sermons constitute the best way to preach about and completely cover the great doctrines of the Bible, each passage relating to the chosen doctrine being expounded so as to cover every aspect of it. The disadvantages are two. First, topical sermons give too much room for oratory and argumentative preaching rather than concentration on the import of the Bible. Secondly, a preacher may choose and develop a topic with passages from the Bible to support it when a careful study will show that the Bible does not intend that teaching; in other words there is the danger of misapplication of Bible passages to support the topic.

subject: LIT
question: Explain what an expository sermon is and discuss its advantages and disadvantages.
idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs; the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is. He must study the passage until its insight is clear to him and allow the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment, paying attention to three elements: statements, which are sentences that report facts; expressions, which demonstrate emotion; and prescriptive sentences, which describe what is to be done. Like the textual sermon it takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text, and references to other texts are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident in the immediate text. The difference between expository and topical preaching is that the former concentrates on a specific text and discusses topics covered in it, while the latter concentrates on a specific topic and finds texts covering that topic. The advantages are these: the main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, since an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period; the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on; expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching; the preacher expounds not a great book, a poem, a political passage or his personal opinion but the authoritative word of God; and the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher. The disadvantages are these: the main disadvantage is that it covers many topics and necessitates often lengthy diversions into other passages for clarification, and does not allow detailed coverage of a particular topic; it is a time-consuming task, and most expository preachers will never cover the entire Bible in their lifetime; exegesis may give way to eisegesis, the art of reading preconceived opinions into the text; and the expositor may wander from the text, stretching and straining it to draw lessons it was never intended to teach, so that instead of expositing the passage the preacher exploits it. The greatest danger of all is that the expositor may fail to proceed from interpretation to application, producing an expository lesson which aims only at the mind instead of an expository sermon which addresses both the mind and the will.

subject: LIT
question: Describe the factors a preacher should observe in the delivery of a sermon.
idealAnswer: After all the spiritual and physical preparation needed in the work of the preacher, one of the important tasks is how to deliver the sermon, for a preacher may write a very good sermon but the effectiveness or the achievement of the desired end of changing lives is largely determined by the delivery. The issues that affect sermon delivery include the appearance of the preacher and his body language, and other manners such as his tone and eye contact. As to appearance, the preacher's appearance has a major impact on the congregation, and the dressing must be decent; while modesty is necessary, it is not good to go to the pulpit shabbily dressed in the name of modesty, and depending on the social status of the congregation the dressing should be generally acceptable and neither offensive nor expensive. The preacher must avoid dresses that draw attention to the preacher rather than the message, and must look cheerful, healthy and fit. As to posture, the preacher must be mindful of how he carries himself, be himself and imitate no one except Christ, be natural in voice and style, and not put his hands in his pockets or on his waist, which carries a wrong impression; he must preach with passion, for a passionate preacher is more likely to make a positive impact than one emotionally detached from the message. As to gesture, the preacher may motion the hands, head and other parts of the body to express or stress points, but this should be done with care; a microphone should be held in the left hand so that the right hand is free for stressing points, remembering that in some cultural settings using the left hand to talk to people is not acceptable, and words like Praise the Lord, halleluiah and Amen should not be used just for the sake of it. As to tone, the preacher must check the tone of his voice and of the message; the gospel is a message of joy, so he must not sound too gloomy even when preaching on sin and repentance, and while some points need a loud voice, it should not be his habit to shout, for he should be heard without shouting and must speak clearly and confidently. The preacher must also involve the congregation by calculated eye contact, looking round to all corners of the chapel, and by verbally involving them, leaving the ends of some quotations to be completed by them, though this must not be abused; he may consult his notes, but staying too glued to them detaches him from the people, and since the average listening capacity spans between ten and twenty five minutes he must be mindful of his time.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss the common problems preachers face in the selection of hymns for service, and suggest how they may be overcome.
idealAnswer: One major problem preachers commonly face is the time to get settled and prepare sermons. Some preachers have always seen sermon preparation as part time or even secondary, and many prepare their sermons on Saturday night or even Sunday morning. Once enough time is not allowed for the sermon preparation, hymn selection will suffer, for the most appropriate time to select hymns is when the sermon has been prepared, or at least when the first draft, outline or sketch is done. A simple suggestion is offered: read the passages latest by Monday evening, keep reflecting on them and on the theme, write points down as they come and gather them by Wednesday night, by which time the preacher may have enough points or ideas to help him select his hymns. Another problem is that most preachers are not familiar with the hymns. We may not know the hymns by their numbers, but at least certain lines should be remembered; the preacher may consult the contents of the Methodist Hymn Book to get an idea of the range of hymns that fit various subjects, and it pays to ask for help from fellow Lay Preachers and Ministers. A third problem is that a number of preachers do not find it easy to understand the theme and find it difficult to link the theme to the passages, let alone to select the appropriate hymns. The remedy is to spend a little more time to reflect and to consult other literature and the help of other preachers, so that we can contribute to a lively and spirit-led worship, but above all to pray for guidance and the Holy Spirit's enlightenment. These problems show themselves in practice when a preacher relies on the same favourite hymns for every appointment without recourse to the theme and lessons, or falls back on 'Tell me the old old story' and 'Lord thy word abideth' as sermon hymns, and on 'Forth in thy name O Lord I go' and 'Now thank we all our God' as closing hymns, because he is not able to select fitting hymns. Since hymns enhance inspirational worship, make participation by all possible and unify the congregation, preachers must approach sermon preparation and hymn selection with all the attention and inspiration they deserve.

subject: LIT
question: Explain the role of each of the four hymns in a Methodist Sunday morning service, and state the factors to consider in choosing the sermon hymn and the closing hymn.
idealAnswer: The first hymn in our services always serves as the hymn of praise and adoration. It is the part of the service that sings the praise of our Maker, and we use it to show our appreciation to God for who He is and what He does; it is therefore amazing to hear people singing 'Faith of our Fathers' or 'Stand up stand up for Jesus' as the first hymn unless the service is a special one that demands it. There is a whole range of hymns that qualify as hymns of praise, the common ones being MHB 1 to MHB 35 and MHB 82 to MHB 116. The second hymn is a hymn of invocation, serving to inspire the worshippers to immerse themselves in the worship and to encourage them to pray; preachers have often chosen from MHB 273 to MHB 301. The third hymn is usually the sermon hymn, sung to prepare the congregation for the day's sermon, and it is expected to be relevant to the sermon by touching on the core or at least an important point of it. Preachers who cannot find a relevant hymn too often fall back on 'Tell me the old old story' or 'Lord thy word abideth', which is not good enough. A hymn wholly expressing the core of the message does not always exist; just a stanza or two, or even a few lines, may be what is needed, and it is the duty of the preacher to show the congregation, during the delivery, that minute part of the hymn which is relevant, by referring to it at the appropriate time. The closing hymn is the hymn of response; it should state the desired response to the sermon and answer the question, what should we do after hearing this sermon? Here again 'Forth in thy name O Lord I go' and the so-called Methodist closing anthem 'Now thank we all our God' have been misused by preachers unable to select fitting hymns of response. Three factors help in choosing the sermon and closing hymns. The first is the theme, which serves as the first point of reflection and, when well understood, gives clues to the hymns, the preacher delimiting which aspect of the theme he will handle. The second is the text, whether the verse or two on which the sermon is anchored or the main passage, or even all three lessons, which when read in the light of the theme give a clue. The third is the proposition, the central thought of the sermon containing the main message and the desired response; it is even thought that the proposition does the best job as an aid to hymn selection. Finally, the preacher must know the special occasion or season on which he is preaching, so that hymns are not sung out of season.

subject: LIT
question: What is prayer? Discuss the four elements which make up the content of prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him; real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God, and this formula is popularly known as CATS, that is Confession, Adoration, Thanksgiving and Supplication, or ACTS, that is Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips. We need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests; to adore God is to display our awareness of His majesty and capability, and as the Psalmist praised God in Psalm 95 for who He is and what He does, this should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed, as Isaiah saw how awful his sins were when he entered the awesome glory of God and confessed them and was purged. Confession of sins must be sincere and specific; it is not a time to tell God hypocritically to forgive unknown sins, but to tell Him also the known and intentional ones, and it must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him, and it enables us to recognize that He controls all things, not just the blessings but the problems and adversities as well; in it the Christian sees God as the creator of a world that was good, the provider of salvation and the giver of every good and perfect thing. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others. Petition is asking God for personal things, since we have varied needs and God has promised to supply them all; intercession is prayer for others, for prayer is not a selfish enterprise but a sharing and caring ministry, and we are to pray for our spouses, children, parents, neighbours, friends, those in authority and our nation. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, and a preacher who does not pray for those he preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

subject: LIT
topic: Background to the Date for Easter Celebration
question: Give an account of the background to the date for the celebration of Easter.
idealAnswer: Easter can be said to have an apostolic background because it derived from a time when Jewish influence was effective, that is the first century A.D., and it depended on the lunar calendar. For three centuries the church tolerated its celebration on different days. While Asia, or the Eastern Orthodox Church, celebrated it on 14 Nisan, others elsewhere had it on the Sunday after 14 Nisan, and both were accepted because they all had apostolic authenticity. Asia therefore celebrated Easter on the same day as the Jewish Passover, and those who kept Easter on the 14th Nisan were known as Quartodecimans. A great controversy, known as the Quartodeciman controversy, erupted as a result of the date of the celebration of Easter, since Asia celebrated it on the 14th Nisan whatever the day of the week, whereas other churches observed it on the Sunday following the 14th Nisan. In 155 AD Polycarp, the Bishop of Smyrna, discussed the matter in Rome with Ancietus and they agreed to differ, so the matter seemed to have rested for some thirty-five years until 190 AD, when Victor of Rome made an energetic attempt to secure uniformity. Because of the large Asiatic population in the capital, one part of the Church was still fasting when the other was feasting. Victor held a Synod and sent out requests for others to meet; though his views were accepted, the Synod of Asia under Polycrates of Ephesus refused to conform, and so Victor stopped communion with Asia. In time the celebration of Easter upon the Sunday was adopted by all, and the only question remaining was whether, in determining the date, the Jewish reckoning was to be followed, as was the custom at Antioch, or whether it should be calculated independently, as was done at Alexandria and Rome. The latter method was the one eventually agreed upon. Easter itself is the oldest and greatest festival in Christianity, falling on the Sunday on which Christ rose from the dead; according to Tertullian it was the normal occasion for converts to be initiated into the Christian faith, so that on Easter Christians commemorated the death and resurrection of Christ and celebrated both baptism and the Eucharist.

subject: LIT
question: State the liturgical colours used in the Christian year and explain the seasons and occasions on which each is used.
idealAnswer: The Christian year contains two cycles: the Christmas Cycle, which is Advent, Christmas and Epiphany, and the Easter Cycle, which is Lent, Easter and Pentecost. Within each cycle there is a preparatory season symbolized by purple and a festival season symbolized by white, and after each cycle there is an ordinary time of growth symbolized by green; thus there is a sequence of seasons using purple, white and green, in that order, twice each year. Purple is a colour of both penitence and royalty, used during the preparatory seasons of Advent and Lent, and blue, a colour of hope, may also be used during Advent. White and gold are joyous and festive colours used during the Christmas and Easter seasons, except on the Day of Pentecost, and in other seasons on festive days such as the Baptism of the Lord, Transfiguration, Trinity, All Saints and Christ the King. White may also be used at weddings and at services where the sacrament of baptism is central, and it is recommended at services of Holy Communion, where white linens on top of the Lord's table are customary, though the perimeter hanging over the sides of the table and other visuals should reflect the day or season of the year. Green is a colour of growth, used in the seasons after Epiphany and after Pentecost, except when special days call for white or red. Red is a colour of fire, symbolizing the Holy Spirit; it is used on the Day of Pentecost and at other times when the work of the Holy Spirit is emphasized, and it is also the colour of the blood of Christ and of the blood of the martyrs. Because of its intensity, red is most effective when used occasionally rather than continuously for a whole season, and it is appropriate for evangelistic services, for ordinations and consecrations, and for church anniversaries and homecomings. It may be used beside white and gold through the Easter season, and during Holy Week, beginning with Passion or Palm Sunday, to symbolize the blood of Christ. Although the use of these colours is based on broad ecumenical tradition, other colours have been and are being used in Christian churches, and creativity with colours and other signs for the days and seasons is encouraged.

subject: LIT
chapter: THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
question: Explain the "unchangeables" and the "changeables" in worship, and discuss how the Church may meet the challenge of making worship culturally relevant.
idealAnswer: Cultural relevance is not about political correctness, nor about watering down the gospel and worship; it is a process by which the church, in its mission of preaching the gospel, becomes culturally sensitive and thus relevant to her context while remaining doctrinally pure. As far as our worship and the gospel are concerned there are unchangeable facts that cannot be compromised, for biblical truths and doctrinal facts are unchangeable: that Christ is the Son of God, that He died to save sinners and that He shall come again to judge the world. The unchangeables are three. The first is Jesus, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever, and the place of God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in our worship does not change. The second is the Word of God, for the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands for ever; the Word gives us our directives for worship, for our lifestyle choices, for practical instruction and for our salvation, so the prominent place of reading and interpreting the Word in our worship cannot change. The third is divine principles, for Titus 1:9 instructs those in leadership to hold firmly to the trustworthy message as it has been taught, and God's truth and the divine principles He has given do not change. The changeables are equally clear. Change comes with age, for we change physically as we age, and while younger people may want a radically different setting with opportunity for self-expression and spontaneous songs, prophecies and revelations, an older congregation may prefer a solemn, reflective and calm setting; we must be sensitive to both and in an intergenerational congregation there must be a fair balance. Ministry methods change, since worship styles, technology, outreach methods and teaching styles are always being adapted: Jesus preached from a boat but we use microphones, Paul wrote on papyrus with a quill but we use computers, the early church studied from scrolls but we have many translations and Bibles on phones, and Paul wore a toga but we wear suits and cassocks. God Himself is a God of change, for the Bible speaks of a new song, a new heaven and earth, new wine, new life, a new covenant, a new creation, a new man and a new command, so the church cannot minister to the people of this millennium with a methodology designed to reach the people of the 1950s. The challenges are met in three ways. First, obtain a biblical worldview, for a worldview is the lenses through which we see our world, and since in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, we will not base our feelings and attitudes on a person's age or social status but will love everyone as God's special creation. Secondly, embrace new methodologies, as Jesus taught in the parables of the old garment and the new wineskins; Jesus embraced what was new and effective and presented truth in the language of His culture, using objects, seeds, soil, coins, camels and fig trees. Thirdly, be creative in worship, for God wants His church to sing a new song; this does not mean we cannot continue praising God with the grand old hymns, nor that we may shut out the new songs, for it is not an either-or but a both-and situation.

subject: LIT
question: Like the textual sermon, the expository sermon takes its subject and main points from a particular text; but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its ______ from the immediate text.
explanation: The sub-points of an expository sermon come from the immediate text itself; other texts only support or confirm it.

manualReference.excerpt:
Expository sermon, like the textual sermon, takes its subject and main points from a 
particular text, but, unlike the textual sermon, it also takes its sub-points from the 
immediate text.
manualReference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Expository Sermons (syllabus ¶3811)

subject: LIT
question: To ______ God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips.
explanation: Adoration is the worship and praise of God, displaying our awareness of His majesty and capability.

manualReference.excerpt: To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips (Ps. 150).
manualReference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — Adoration (syllabus ¶3962)

subject: LIT
question: Preparation for Easter, originally two days of prayer and fasting, was lengthened to a week and then to 40 days, now called ______ in English.
explanation: The forty-day preparation for Easter grew out of a two-day fast and is called Lent in English.

manualReference.excerpt:
Previously, 
preparation for Easter spanned over two days, with prayer and fasting i.e. on Friday and 
Saturday. This was lengthened to a week and then to 40 days now called Lent in English.
manualReference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — EASTER (syllabus ¶4002)
